subtype: Hiraeth for a home and language left behind [Actor]
passage:
By three in the afternoon the Stockholm sky was already dark, and the corridor smelled of Oskar's saffron buns for Lucia. Zanele sat on her bed, playing a voice note from her gogo for the fourth time, just to hear isiZulu spoken properly.
At home it would be hot now, the December holidays starting, cousins arriving in minibus taxis, the whole street smelling of braai smoke. She could see every dusty lane of Eshowe, every jacaranda. In her memory nobody ever argued, the power never failed, and the church choir never once sang off-key.
Oskar knocked. "Lucia procession tonight? Candles, songs. You'll like it."
"Maybe," she said, and smiled, but her throat was tight. The songs would be beautiful. They just wouldn't be hers.

qa.q: Whose voice note was Zanele playing?
qa.a: A voice note from her gogo, for the fourth time.

qa.q: What is Zanele feeling as she replays the voice note?
qa.a: She feels a deep ache of longing for her language and town, homesick enough that her throat tightens even at a kind invitation.

qa.q: What could help Zanele with the longing this December?
qa.a: She could go to the Lucia procession with Oskar and also call home, perhaps teaching Oskar an isiZulu song, so she carries home into the new place.

qa.q: How might Oskar see Zanele's "Maybe"?
qa.a: Oskar may think Zanele is just tired, not knowing how far away home feels, or may notice the tight smile and gently ask again.

grounding: A student far from home aches for her language, lanes and festivals, remembered as more perfect than they were.

subtype: Longing for a place that may no longer exist [Actor]
passage:
Hockey club log, Baisakhi, 13 April. Gurpreet (coach)
Tarun came by today, first time in four years, down from his job in Bengaluru. Twenty-five now, a jacket over his kurta. He walked straight to where the old mud ground used to be and stood looking at the new parking lot for a long time. Asked about Sharma ji's dhaba; I told him it shut two winters ago. He laughed, but it didn't reach his eyes. "I kept thinking I'd come back and it would all be here," he said. "Even me. The old me."
I walked him to the new turf behind the school and let him take a few shots with the juniors. He hit the post twice and grinned properly then. Invited him to the evening match; he said he would try.

qa.q: What stands where the old mud ground used to be?
qa.a: A new parking lot.

qa.q: What does Tarun's laugh that "didn't reach his eyes" suggest?
qa.a: He feels a sad, wistful ache, longing not just for the ground and the dhaba but for the old self and time he hoped to find there.

qa.q: How did the coach respond, and why might it help?
qa.a: The coach walked Tarun to the new turf and let him play with the juniors, giving him a way to connect with the town as it is now, not only as it was.

qa.q: What would change if the ground and the dhaba were still there?
qa.a: Tarun might feel comforted for a while, but he would likely still miss the time and the younger self he hoped to find, which no place can give back.

grounding: A young professional returns to a changed hometown and finds the longing is for a time and a younger self as much as a place.

subtype: Parent at home yearning for the grown child [Observer]
passage:
Note for Naveen, left in the family diary, Sunday
Bhaijaan, you asked how Ammi is. Mostly fine. But here is what I saw this week. Every morning she dusts your room, though nobody has slept there since you left for Toronto in March. She changed the bedsheet on Friday, "in case". Twice I found her standing at your graduation photo on the landing, holding the duster, not dusting. When your call came on Wednesday she laughed at everything you said, then sat quietly on your bed for an hour.
So I've done something. I have fixed a Sunday video call, eight in the evening here, your morning. Please keep it. It isn't about news. She just needs to see your face.
Parveen

qa.q: When did Naveen leave for Toronto?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: What does Parveen feel watching Ammi at the photograph?
qa.a: Parveen feels tender and a little worried, seeing that Ammi's love has turned into quiet waiting, which is why the Sunday calls were fixed.

qa.q: Why might a fixed Sunday call help more than occasional ones?
qa.a: It gives Ammi something to look forward to; as the note says, it isn't about news, she just needs to see Naveen's face.

qa.q: How does Ammi seem to experience Naveen's absence?
qa.a: Ammi misses him deeply and shows it by waiting: dusting his room, changing the sheet "in case" and standing still at his photograph.

grounding: A young adult sees a parent keep the absent son's room ready and pause at his photograph, and sets up regular calls.

subtype: Carrying home while building a new one [Response]
passage:
Francis had been the agriculture officer in Wardha for eight months when his first Christmas away came round. On Sunday he video-called Mae in Margao, holding the phone up so she could see the paper star on his window. "It's crooked," she laughed, wiping her eyes.
That evening he did not sit alone. He had invited Jeevan from the seed office, Jeevan's wife and two kids, and the old tailor from downstairs. He cooked Mae's chicken xacuti from her voice notes, with too much chilli, and Jeevan brought puran poli. The kids hung paper chains while the tailor told stories of village fairs.
Later, washing up, Francis hummed a Konkani carol. He missed Goa, sharply. But the house was full, and it was his.

qa.q: What dish did Francis cook from Mae's voice notes?
qa.a: Chicken xacuti, with too much chilli.

qa.q: How does Francis feel while washing up and humming the carol?
qa.a: He misses Goa sharply, yet feels warm and content because the house is full and feels like his own.

qa.q: Which choices helped Francis carry home while building a new one?
qa.a: The video call and paper star kept the ritual alive, and inviting Jeevan's family and the tailor made the festival meal a way to build friendships where he lives.

qa.q: What might the evening have meant to Jeevan's family?
qa.a: For Jeevan's family it was likely a warm welcome into a colleague's festival, and a chance to share their own puran poli in return.

grounding: An adult far from home keeps a festival meal and calls alive while inviting new neighbours in.

passage:
At the nursery in the Kondapur apartment block, Lavanya dropped her biscuit and wailed. Across the mat, Alka looked up from her blocks. Her lip trembled. Then she wailed too, big tears rolling, though her own biscuit was safe in her hand.
Her cousin Rudra, there with Chitti for pick-up, stared. "Why is Alka crying? Nothing happened to her!"
Chitti scooped both girls up. "Sometimes tears just jump across," she said, rocking them.

qa.q: What did Lavanya drop?
qa.a: Her biscuit.

qa.q: Why does Alka start crying when her own biscuit is safe?
qa.a: She catches Lavanya's upset without knowing why; seeing Lavanya wail makes Alka feel upset too.

qa.q: What helps both toddlers in this moment?
qa.a: Chitti's calm response, picking both girls up and rocking them, soothes the shared upset without needing a reason.

qa.q: How does Rudra see Alka's tears?
qa.a: Rudra is puzzled, since nothing happened to Alka, and does not yet understand how feelings can spread between little children.

grounding: A toddler bursts into tears when another child cries, and her cousin is puzzled by it.

subtype: Embarrassed for a friend who is called out [Actor]
passage:
The week of the village jatra, nobody in Class 5 had slept much; the giant wheel had creaked till midnight. In the first period, Sir held up Irawati's empty notebook.
"Again? Stand up. Tell everyone why."
Irawati stood, fingers twisting her plait. Two rows behind, Jahnavi's cheeks went hot. Her stomach clenched as if it were her own name being called. She stared at her slate, curled her toes inside her chappals, and wished the bench would swallow her.
When Irawati sat down, Jahnavi slid a tamarind sweet across under the desk without looking up. Irawati took it. Neither of them said a word.

qa.q: What did Sir hold up in the first period?
qa.a: Irawati's empty notebook.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling while Irawati stood?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt embarrassed and ashamed as if it were her own name, cheeks hot and stomach clenched, wishing the bench would swallow her.

qa.q: What small kindness did Jahnavi find, and why does it fit?
qa.a: She slid Irawati a tamarind sweet without a word, a quiet way of saying "I'm with you" that adds no more attention.

qa.q: What would change if Sir had spoken to Irawati privately?
qa.a: Irawati might have felt less humiliated, and Jahnavi would not have felt the shame in her own body from two rows away.

grounding: A child squirms and burns with shame when her friend is scolded in class, feeling it as her own.

subtype: Thrill at a team's win or a character's fate [Actor]
passage:
Chapchar Kut dancers were still stamping between the bamboo poles on the ground below when Lalremsiami and Devika crouched behind the stage with one phone and one bar of signal. The under-19 final, last over. Six needed off two balls.
The stream froze. Lalremsiami's heart hammered so hard she could feel it in her ears. "Come on, come on," she whispered, shaking the phone as if that would help.
"Hold it higher!" Devika hissed, climbing onto a crate.
The picture jerked back: the ball sailing over long-on. Both girls shrieked, grabbed each other and jumped till the crate tipped over. A dancer turned and laughed at them.
Lalremsiami had never met a single player on that team. It still felt like her own win.

qa.q: How many runs were needed, and off how many balls?
qa.a: Six needed off two balls.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when the stream froze?
qa.a: She felt tense and desperate, her heart hammering in her ears, as if the result were her own.

qa.q: What does this scene show about watching a match together?
qa.a: Sharing the tension with Devika made the joy bigger; feeling with a team connects fans, as long as a loss is not taken too personally.

qa.q: How did Devika share in the moment?
qa.a: Devika was just as caught up, climbing a crate for signal and shrieking and jumping with Lalremsiami when the six landed.

grounding: A teenager's heart pounds through a cricket final's last over as though the win were her own.

subtype: Absorbing strangers' pain from the news feed [Actor]
passage:
Sunday, late May. The fan barely stirred the hot air in the PG room. Kashish lay scrolling: a flooded village somewhere, a father crying outside a hospital, a building fire, a lost dog. Story after story. At 2 a.m. her jaw ached from clenching.
Monday. At the internship, Sahil asked, "Lunch at the dhaba?" and she snapped, "Can you not?" then stared at her screen, heavy and irritable, unable to say why.
Wednesday. The same scrolling each night, the same knot each morning. On the metro Sahil said quietly, "Rough week?"
"That's the weird part," Kashish said. "Nothing happened to me. I just feel soaked. Like I'm carrying stuff I can't do anything about."

qa.q: At what time did Kashish's jaw ache from clenching?
qa.a: At 2 a.m. on Sunday night.

qa.q: Why does Kashish snap at Sahil on Monday?
qa.a: She feels tense and low from soaking up strangers' pain all night, heavy and irritable without knowing why, so a simple lunch question feels like too much.

qa.q: What small step could help Kashish this week?
qa.a: Set a cut-off time for scrolling, pick one small thing she can actually do for a cause she saw, and talk it through with Sahil.

qa.q: What might Sahil notice by Wednesday?
qa.a: Sahil has likely noticed that she is snappy and heavy, and cares enough to ask "Rough week?" instead of taking Monday's snap personally.

grounding: A young adult absorbs distressing stories from her feed and feels tense and low for days without knowing why.

subtype: Feeling with others without taking the feeling over [Response]
passage:
Imran: how was day 1 at the shelter?
Akash: heavy. a girl told me about the night they lost their house in the fire
Akash: came home and couldn't stop replaying it
Imran: that sounds really hard
Akash: my supervisor said something useful though. "feel it with them, don't carry it for them"
Akash: so I'm trying. this is her grief, not mine. I can care without making it mine
Imran: that's wise honestly
Akash: also putting my phone away tonight. no news, just dal and a walk
Akash: and tomorrow I'm bringing a box of storybooks. she said she misses her books
Imran: I've got about 20 kids' books from my nephew. want them?
Akash: yes! that would actually help

qa.q: What will Akash bring to the shelter tomorrow?
qa.a: A box of storybooks.

qa.q: How was Akash feeling after the first day?
qa.a: Akash felt heavy and shaken, replaying the girl's story, but also steadier after remembering "feel it with them, don't carry it for them".

qa.q: Which of Akash's steps would help anyone who works with others' pain?
qa.a: Naming the feeling as the girl's grief rather than Akash's own, taking a break from the phone and news, and turning the care into one small act like bringing books.

qa.q: How might the girl at the shelter feel when the storybooks arrive?
qa.a: She would likely feel remembered and comforted, since she said she missed her books and someone listened. 🤍

grounding: An adult separates a child's grief from their own, takes a break and turns the feeling into a small act of help.

subtype: Child freezes and cries at a friend's fall [Actor]
passage:
Janmashtami evening, and the colony courtyard was strung with marigolds for the dahi handi. Sachin raced Parul to the slide, tripped on a loose tile and landed hard. His knee was bleeding.
Parul stopped dead. Her mouth opened and a huge wail came out, louder than Sachin's. She stood rooted, hands flapping, eyes squeezed shut. She wanted Sachin to be okay. She just couldn't make her legs move.
The watchman uncle came running with a water bottle. Parul was still crying when Sachin, sniffing, was already sitting up.

qa.q: What did Sachin trip on?
qa.a: A loose tile.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling as she stood rooted?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and frightened for Sachin; she wanted him to be okay, but her own distress was so big she couldn't move.

qa.q: How could an adult help Parul after this?
qa.a: Hold her until she calms, tell her it was kind to feel sad for Sachin, and practise one simple thing to do next time, like shouting "Help!" or fetching a grown-up.

qa.q: What might Sachin have noticed while sitting up?
qa.a: That Parul was crying louder than he was, and perhaps that his friend was upset for him even though she could not come to help.

grounding: A child sees her friend fall and is so swamped by her own distress that she cries and cannot move to help.
